lesson.title: From Blueprint to Reality: What Objects Are
lesson.summary: An object is one concrete instance built from a class's blueprint, with its own independent existence and its own copy of whatever data the class describes.
lesson.body:
A class describes what a dog should look like in general, but it does not create any actual dogs by itself, the same way a house blueprint does not put a roof over anyone's head until someone actually builds a house from it. An object is what you get when you use a class to build one concrete thing that matches that description. Each object is entirely its own entity: it exists separately in memory from every other object built from the same class, and changing one object does not affect any other.

```python
class Dog:
    pass

rex = Dog()
fido = Dog()

print(rex is fido)

rex.name = "Rex"
fido.name = "Fido"
print(rex.name, fido.name)
```

```
False
Rex Fido
```

Calling Dog() creates a brand new object each time, so even though rex and fido were built from the exact same class, rex is fido evaluates to False: they are two distinct objects, not the same one referred to by two names. That independence is exactly why attaching a name attribute to rex has no effect on fido; each object keeps its own separate attributes.

The words "object" and "instance" are used interchangeably in Python: rex is an object, and rex is also an instance of the Dog class, meaning it is one of potentially many things built from that particular blueprint. The act of building an object from a class, the moment Dog() actually runs, is called instantiation, and it is worth its own close look, since a lot happens in that single line of code.
